{{Short description|Mathematical inequality explaining concentration of random variables}}
In [[probability theory]], '''concentration inequalities''' provide mathematical bounds on the probability of a [[random variable]] deviating from some value (typically, its [[expected value]]). The deviation or other function of the random variable can be thought of as a secondary random variable. The simplest example of the concentration of such a secondary random variable is the CDF of the first random variable which concentrates the probability to unity. If an analytic form of the CDF is available this provides a concentration '''equality''' that provides the exact probability of concentration. It is precisely when the CDF is difficult to calculate or even the exact form of the first random variable is unknown that the applicable concentration inequalities provide useful insight.

Another almost universal example of a secondary random variable is the [[law of large numbers]] of classical probability theory which states that sums of independent random variables, under mild conditions, concentrate around their expectation with a high probability. Such sums are the most basic examples of random variables concentrated around their [[mean]].

Concentration inequalities can be sorted according to how much information about the random variable is needed in order to use them.{{Citation needed|date=December 2023}}

==Markov's inequality==
{{Main|Markov's inequality}}
Let <math>X</math> be a random variable that is non-negative ([[almost surely]]). Then, for every constant <math>a > 0</math>,

: <math>\Pr(X \geq a) \leq \frac{\operatorname{E}(X)}{a}.</math>

Note the following extension to Markov's inequality: if <math>\Phi</math> is a strictly increasing and non-negative function, then

:<math>\Pr(X \geq a) = \Pr(\Phi (X) \geq \Phi (a)) \leq \frac{\operatorname{E}(\Phi(X))}{\Phi (a)}.</math>

== Chebyshev's inequality ==
{{Main|Chebyshev's inequality}}
Chebyshev's inequality requires the following information on a random variable <math>X</math>:

* The expected value <math>\operatorname{E}[X]</math> is finite.
* The [[variance]] <math>\operatorname{Var}[X] = \operatorname{E}[(X - \operatorname{E}[X] )^2]</math> is finite.

Then, for every constant <math>a > 0</math>,

:<math>\Pr(|X-\operatorname{E}[X]| \geq a) \leq \frac{\operatorname{Var}[X]}{a^2},</math>

or equivalently,

:<math>\Pr(|X-\operatorname{E}[X]| \geq a\cdot \operatorname{Std}[X]) \leq \frac{1}{a^2},</math>

where <math>\operatorname{Std}[X]</math> is the [[standard deviation]] of <math>X</math>.

Chebyshev's inequality can be seen as a special case of the generalized Markov's inequality applied to the random variable <math>|X-\operatorname{E}[X]|</math> with <math>\Phi(x) = x^2</math>.

== Vysochanskij–Petunin inequality ==
{{Main|Vysochanskij–Petunin inequality}}Let ''X'' be a random variable with unimodal distribution, mean ''μ'' and finite, non-zero variance ''σ''<sup>2</sup>. Then, for any <math display="inline">\lambda > \sqrt{\frac{8}{3}} = 1.63299\ldots,</math>

: <math>\Pr(\left|X-\mu\right|\geq \lambda\sigma)\leq\frac{4}{9\lambda^2}.</math>

(For a relatively elementary proof see e.g. <ref>[https://www.jstor.org/stable/pdf/2684253.pdf Pukelsheim, F., 1994. The Three Sigma Rule. ''The American Statistician'', 48(2), pp. 88–91]</ref>).

=== One-sided Vysochanskij–Petunin inequality ===
For a unimodal random variable <math>X</math> and <math>r\geq0</math>, the one-sided Vysochanskij–Petunin inequality<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Mercadier |first1=Mathieu |last2=Strobel |first2=Frank |date=2021-11-16 |title=A one-sided Vysochanskii–Petunin inequality with financial applications |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0377221721001545 |journal=European Journal of Operational Research |language=en |volume=295 |issue=1 |pages=374–377 |doi=10.1016/j.ejor.2021.02.041 |issn=0377-2217}}</ref> holds as follows:

: <math>\Pr(X-E[X]\geq r)\leq
	\begin{cases}
		\dfrac{4}{9}\dfrac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{r^2 + \operatorname{Var}(X)} & \text{for }r^2 \geq\dfrac{5}{3} \operatorname{Var}(X),\\[5pt]
		\dfrac{4}{3}\dfrac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{r^2 + \operatorname{Var}(X)}-\dfrac{1}{3} & \text{otherwise.}
	\end{cases}
</math>

== Paley–Zygmund inequality ==
{{Main|Paley–Zygmund inequality}}
In contrast to most commonly used concentration inequalities, the Paley-Zygmund inequality provides a ''lower'' bound on the deviation probability.

==Chernoff bounds==
{{Main|Chernoff bound}}
The generic Chernoff bound<ref name="MitzenmacherUpfal">{{cite book | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=0bAYl6d7hvkC | title=Probability and Computing: Randomized Algorithms and Probabilistic Analysis | publisher=Cambridge University Press |author1=Mitzenmacher, Michael  |author1-link=Michael Mitzenmacher |author2=Upfal, Eli |author2-link=Eli Upfal |year=2005 |isbn=0-521-83540-2}}</ref>{{rp|63–65}} requires the [[moment generating function]] of <math>X</math>, defined as <math>M_X(t):=\operatorname{E}\!\left[e^{tX}\right].</math> It always exists, but may be infinite. From Markov's inequality, for every <math>t>0</math>:

:<math>\Pr(X \geq a) \leq \frac{\operatorname{E}[e^{tX}]}{e^{ta}},</math>

and for every <math>t<0</math>:

:<math>\Pr(X \leq a) \leq \frac{\operatorname{E}[e^{tX}]}{e^{ta}}.</math>

There are various Chernoff bounds for different distributions and different values of the parameter <math>t</math>. See <ref name="OneHundredNPS">{{cite news | title=One Hundred Statistics and Probability Inequalities |author1=Slagle, N.P.  | year=2012| arxiv=2102.07234 }}</ref>{{rp|5–7}} for a compilation of more concentration inequalities.

== Mill's inequality ==
Let <math>Z \sim N(0,\sigma^2)</math>. Then for every <math>t>0</math> we have that:<ref name="MillsInequality">{{cite web | author = Addison Hu | title = Mill's Inequality | url = http://huisaddison.com/blog/mills-inequality.html | website = Addison Hu | access-date = 2025-05-14}}</ref>

:<math display="block">\operatorname{P} (|Z| > t) \le \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}} \frac{\sigma}{t} \exp(-\frac{t^2}{2\sigma^2}).</math>

== Bounds on sums of independent bounded variables ==
{{Main|Hoeffding's inequality|Azuma's inequality|McDiarmid's inequality|Bennett's inequality|Bernstein inequalities (probability theory)}}
Let <math>X_1, X_2,\dots,X_n</math> be independent random variables such that, for all ''i'':
:<math>a_i\leq X_i\leq b_i</math> [[almost surely]].
:<math>c_i := b_i-a_i</math>
:<math>\forall i: c_i \leq C</math>
Let <math>S_n</math> be their sum, <math>E_n</math> its [[expected value]] and <math>V_n</math> its variance:
:<math>S_n := \sum_{i=1}^n X_i</math>
:<math>E_n := \operatorname{E}[S_n] = \sum_{i=1}^n \operatorname{E}[X_i]</math>
:<math>V_n := \operatorname{Var}[S_n] = \sum_{i=1}^n \operatorname{Var}[X_i]</math>

It is often interesting to bound the difference between the sum and its expected value. Several inequalities can be used.

1. [[Hoeffding's inequality]] says that:
::<math>\Pr\left[|S_n-E_n|>t\right] \le 2 \exp \left(-\frac{2t^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n c_i^2} \right) \le 2 \exp \left(-\frac{2t^2}{n C^2} \right)</math>

2. The random variable <math>S_n-E_n</math> is a special case of a [[martingale (probability theory)|martingale]], and <math>S_0-E_0=0</math>. Hence, the general form of [[Azuma's inequality]] can also be used and it yields a similar bound:
::<math>\Pr\left[|S_n-E_n|>t\right] < 2 \exp \left(-\frac{2t^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n c_i^2}\right)< 2 \exp \left(-\frac{2t^2}{n C^2} \right) </math>
This is a generalization of Hoeffding's since it can handle other types of martingales, as well as [[supermartingale]]s and [[submartingale]]s. See  Fan et al. (2015).<ref name=fan>{{cite journal |title=Exponential inequalities for martingales with applications| first1=X. |last1=Fan|  first2=I. |last2=Grama | first3=Q. |last3=Liu | journal=Electronic Journal of Probability |publisher=Electron. J. Probab. 20| year=2015| volume=20 | pages=1–22| url=http://projecteuclid.org/euclid.ejp/1465067107 | doi=10.1214/EJP.v20-3496|arxiv=1311.6273}}</ref> Note that if the simpler form of Azuma's inequality is used, the exponent in the bound is worse by a factor of 4.

3. The sum function, <math>S_n=f(X_1,\dots,X_n)</math>, is a special case of a function of ''n'' variables. This function changes in a bounded way: if variable ''i'' is changed, the value of ''f'' changes by at most <math>b_i-a_i<C</math>. Hence, [[McDiarmid's inequality]] can also be used and it yields a similar bound:
::<math>\Pr\left[|S_n-E_n|>t\right] < 2 \exp \left(-\frac{2t^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n c_i^2} \right)< 2 \exp \left(-\frac{2t^2}{n C^2} \right)</math>
This is a different generalization of Hoeffding's since it can handle other functions besides the sum function, as long as they change in a bounded way.

4. [[Bennett's inequality]] offers some improvement over Hoeffding's when the variances of the summands are small compared to their almost-sure bounds ''C''. It says that:
::<math>\Pr\left[|S_n-E_n| > t \right] \leq
2\exp\left[ - \frac{V_n}{C^2} h\left(\frac{C t}{V_n} \right)\right],</math> where <math>h(u) = (1+u)\log(1+u)-u</math>

5. The first of [[Bernstein inequalities (probability theory)|Bernstein's inequalities]] says that:
::<math>\Pr\left[|S_n-E_n|>t\right] < 2 \exp \left(-\frac{t^2/2}{V_n + C\cdot t/3} \right)</math>
This is a generalization of Hoeffding's since it can handle random variables with not only almost-sure bound but both almost-sure bound and variance bound.

6. Chernoff bounds have a particularly simple form in the case of sum of independent variables, since <math>\operatorname{E}[e^{t\cdot S_n}] = \prod_{i=1}^n {\operatorname{E}[e^{t\cdot X_i}]}</math>.

For example,<ref name=ChungChernoff>{{cite web|last1=Chung|first1=Fan| author1-link= Fan Chung | first2= Linyuan  | last2=Lu |title=Old and new concentration inequalities|url=http://www.math.ucsd.edu/~fan/complex/ch2.pdf|work= Complex Graphs and Networks | publisher= [[American Mathematical Society]] | year= 2010 |accessdate=August 14, 2018}}</ref> suppose the variables <math>X_i</math> satisfy <math>X_i \geq E(X_i)-a_i-M</math>, for <math>1 \leq i \leq n</math>. Then we have lower tail inequality:
::<math>\Pr[S_n - E_n < -\lambda]\leq \exp\left(-\frac{\lambda^2}{2(V_n+\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2+M\lambda/3)}\right)</math>

If <math>X_i</math> satisfies <math>X_i \leq E(X_i)+a_i+M</math>, we have upper tail inequality:
::<math>\Pr[S_n - E_n > \lambda]\leq \exp\left(-\frac{\lambda^2}{2(V_n + \sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2+M\lambda/3)}\right)</math>

If <math>X_i</math> are i.i.d., <math>|X_i| \leq 1</math> and <math>\sigma^2</math> is the variance of <math>X_i</math>, a typical version of Chernoff inequality is:
::<math>\Pr[|S_n| \geq k\sigma]\leq 2e^{-k^2/4n} \text{ for } 0 \leq k\leq 2\sigma.</math>

7. Similar bounds can be found in: [[Rademacher distribution#Bounds on sums]]

==Efron–Stein inequality==
The Efron–Stein inequality (or influence inequality, or MG bound on variance) bounds the variance of a general function.

Suppose that <math>X_1 \dots X_n</math>, <math>X_1' \dots X_n'</math> are independent with <math>X_i'</math> and <math>X_i</math> having the same distribution for all <math>i</math>.

Let <math>X = (X_1,\dots , X_n), X^{(i)} = (X_1, \dots , X_{i-1}, X_i',X_{i+1}, \dots , X_n).</math> Then

: <math>
\mathrm{Var}(f(X)) \leq \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{n} E[(f(X)-f(X^{(i)}))^2].
</math>

A proof may be found in e.g., <ref>{{cite journal |last1=Boucheron |first1=Stéphane |last2=Lugosi |first2=Gábor |last3=Bousquet |first3=Olivier |title=Concentration inequalities |journal=Advanced Lectures on Machine Learning: ML Summer Schools 2003, Canberra, Australia, February 2–14, 2003, Tübingen, Germany, August 4–16, 2003, Revised Lectures |date=2004 |pages=208–240 |publisher=Springer}}</ref>.

== Bretagnolle–Huber–Carol inequality ==
[[Bretagnolle–Huber inequality|Bretagnolle–Huber–Carol Inequality]] bounds the difference between a vector of [[Multinomial distribution|multinomially distributed random variables]] and a vector of expected values.<ref name="Bretagnolle">{{cite book |author1=Bretagnolle, Jean |url=http://www.numdam.org/item/SPS_1978__12__332_0/ |title=Séminaire de Probabilités XII |author2=Huber-Carol, Catherine |chapter=Lois empiriques et distance de Prokhorov |year=1978 |isbn=978-3-540-08761-8 |series=Lecture Notes in Mathematics |volume=649 |pages=332–341 |doi=10.1007/BFb0064609}}</ref><ref name="Vaart">{{cite book |author1=van der Vaart, A.W.|author1-link=Aad van der Vaart|author2=Wellner, J.A.|author2-link=Jon A. Wellner|title = Weak convergence and empirical processes: With applications to statistics| publisher= Springer Science & Business Media|year = 1996}}</ref>
A simple proof appears in <ref name="Ushioda">{{cite journal | author1=Yuto Ushioda|author2=Masato Tanaka|author3=Tomomi Matsui|title= Monte Carlo Methods for the Shapley–Shubik Power Index|journal=Games | volume=13 | issue=3 | pages=44 |year=2022|doi= 10.3390/g13030044 |doi-access=free |arxiv=2101.02841 }}</ref>(Appendix Section).

If a random vector <math>(Z_1, Z_2, Z_3, \ldots , Z_n) </math> 
is multinomially distributed with parameters 
<math> (p_1, p_2, \ldots , p_ n) </math>
and satisfies <math> Z_1 + Z_2 + \dots + Z_n = M, </math> 
then 
::<math> \Pr\left( \sum_{i=1}^n |Z_i -M p_i|  \geq 2M \varepsilon \right)
   \leq 2^n e^{-2M\varepsilon^2}. </math>

This inequality  is used to bound the [[Total variation distance of probability measures|total variation distance]].

== Mason and van Zwet inequality ==

The Mason and van Zwet inequality<ref name=Mason>{{cite journal | author1=Mason, David M.| author2=Willem R. Van Zwet | author2-link=Willem van Zwet | title= A Refinement of the KMT Inequality for the Uniform Empirical Process | journal=The Annals of Probability | volume=15 | issue=3 | year = 1987 | pages= 871–884 | doi=10.1214/aop/1176992070 | doi-access=free }}</ref> for multinomial random vectors concerns a slight modification of the classical chi-square statistic.

Let the random vector <math>(N_1, \ldots ,N_k) </math> be multinomially distributed with parameters <math>n </math> and <math>(p_1,\ldots , p_k)</math> such that <math> p_i > 0</math> for <math> i < k.</math> Then for every <math>C > 0 </math> and <math> \delta > 0 </math> 
there exist constants <math> a, b, c > 0,</math> such that for all <math> n \geq 1</math>  and <math> \lambda ,p_1, \ldots , p_{k-1} </math> 
satisfying <math> \lambda > Cn \min \{p_i | 1 \leq i \leq k-1 \} </math> and <math>  \sum_{i=1}^{k-1} p_i \leq 1 -\delta, </math> we have 
::<math> \Pr\left( \sum_{i=1}^{k-1} \frac{(N_i-np_i)^2}{np_i}> \lambda \right)
   \leq a e^{bk-c\lambda}. </math>

== Dvoretzky–Kiefer–Wolfowitz inequality ==
{{Main|Dvoretzky–Kiefer–Wolfowitz inequality}}

The Dvoretzky–Kiefer–Wolfowitz inequality bounds the difference between the real and the empirical [[cumulative distribution function]].

Given a natural number <math>n</math>, let <math>X_1, X_2,\dots,X_n</math> be real-valued [[independent and identically distributed]] [[random variable]]s with [[cumulative distribution function]] ''F''(·).  Let <math>F_n</math> denote the associated [[empirical distribution function]] defined by
:<math>F_n(x) = \frac1n \sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf{1}_{\{X_i\leq x\}},\qquad x\in\mathbb{R}.</math>
So <math>F(x)</math> is the probability that a ''single'' random variable <math>X</math> is smaller than <math>x</math>, and <math>F_n(x)</math> is the ''average number'' of random variables that are smaller than <math>x</math>.

Then
::<math>\Pr\left(\sup_{x\in\mathbb R} \bigl(F_n(x) - F(x)\bigr) > \varepsilon \right) \le e^{-2n\varepsilon^2} \text{ for every } \varepsilon \geq \sqrt{\tfrac 1 {2n} \ln2}.</math>

==Anti-concentration inequalities==
'''Anti-concentration inequalities''', on the other hand, provide an ''upper bound'' on how much a random variable can concentrate, either on a specific value or range of values. A concrete example is that if you flip a [[fair coin]] <math>n</math> times, the probability that any given number of heads appears will be less than <math>\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}</math>. This idea can be greatly generalized. For example, a result of Rao and Yehudayoff<ref name="RaoYehudayoff">{{cite news | url=https://eccc.weizmann.ac.il/report/2018/194/ | title=Anti-concentration in most directions | publisher=Electronic Colloquium on Computational Complexity |author1=Rao, Anup  |author2=Yehudayoff, Amir | year=2018}}</ref> implies that for any <math>\beta, \delta > 0</math> there exists some <math>C > 0</math> such that, for any <math>k</math>, the following is true for at least <math>2^{n(1 - \delta)}</math> values of <math>x \in \{\pm 1\}^n</math>:
::<math>
\Pr\left(\langle x, Y\rangle = k\right) \le \frac{C}{\sqrt{n}},
</math>
where <math>Y</math> is drawn uniformly from <math>\{\pm 1\}^n</math>.

Such inequalities are of importance in several fields, including [[communication complexity]] (''e.g.'', in proofs of the [[Gap-Hamming problem|gap&nbsp;Hamming problem]]<ref name="Sherstov">{{cite news | url=https://theoryofcomputing.org/articles/v008a008/ | title=The Communication Complexity of Gap Hamming Distance | publisher=[[Theory of Computing]] |author1=Sherstov, Alexander A. | year=2012}}</ref>) and [[graph theory]].<ref name="Kwan">{{cite journal | title=Anticoncentration for subgraph statistics | journal=Journal of the London Mathematical Society | volume=99 | issue=3 | pages=757–777 |author1=Matthew Kwan | author2=Benny Sudakov | author2-link=Benny Sudakov | author3= Tuan Tran | year=2018| doi=10.1112/jlms.12192 | bibcode=2018arXiv180705202K | arxiv=1807.05202 | s2cid=54065186 }}</ref>

An interesting anti-concentration inequality for weighted sums of independent [[Rademacher distribution|Rademacher]] random variables can be obtained using the [[Paley–Zygmund inequality|Paley–Zygmund]] and the [[Khintchine inequality|Khintchine]] inequalities.<ref name="Veraar">{{cite arXiv |eprint = 0909.2586v1|last1 = Veraar|first1 = Mark|title = On Khintchine inequalities with a weight|class = math.PR|year = 2009}}</ref>

Yet another useful anti-concentration result is the Kolmogorov–Rogozin inequality for sums of independent summands. <ref>{{Cite journal |last=Juškevičius |first=Tomas |date=November 2024 |title=The sharp form of the Kolmogorov–Rogozin inequality and a conjecture of Leader–Radcliffe |url=https://londmathsoc.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1112/blms.13132 |journal=Bulletin of the London Mathematical Society |language=en |volume=56 |issue=11 |pages=3289–3299 |doi=10.1112/blms.13132 |issn=0024-6093}}</ref>
